sections.markdown:
## C — Special driving conditions: night driving and beam distances, headlight law, snow and ice, wet pavement, hydroplaning, anti-lock brakes, skids, fog, and emergencies from brake failure and blowouts to stalling on railroad tracks
Knowledge domain: how to drive and use headlights at night and in bad weather, how to start, brake and keep distance on snow and ice, why wet roads and hydroplaning cut traction, how to brake with anti-lock brakes, how to recover from a skid, how to handle fog, and the step-by-step responses to common vehicle emergencies.

FACT_ID: sec11-F01 | anchor: A01
Night driving is harder because headlights show less of the road ahead and to the sides than daylight does, and oncoming glare makes the road harder to see. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F02 | anchor: A01
Headlights must be on from half an hour after sunset until half an hour before sunrise. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F03 | anchor: A01
Keep windows and headlights clean, make sure the lights work, and have their aim checked from time to time. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F04 | anchor: A01
Use high beams whenever no vehicles are coming toward you. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F05 | anchor: A01
Headlights let you see only about 350 feet ahead, so do not overdrive them; keep a speed at which you can stop or turn within that range. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F06 | anchor: A01
Dim to low beams within 500 feet, about one block, of an oncoming vehicle, and within 300 feet when following another vehicle. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F07 | anchor: A01
At night, follow the edgeline, or the center line if there is no edgeline, and watch for signs and for people and vehicles stopped beside the road. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F08 | anchor: A01
Missouri requires headlights any time the weather calls for using your windshield wipers. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F09 | anchor: A01
In winter clear all snow and ice from the windows, headlights and taillights, and never set off, however short the trip, until the windows are clear. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F10 | anchor: A01
Snow-rated tires or chains help, but no vehicle can be driven safely on snow or ice at normal speeds, so slow down and do not use cruise control. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F11 | anchor: A01
If your tires spin when starting on snow, rock gently back and forth to clear a path, then spread salt, sand or cat litter around the wheels if needed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F12 | anchor: A01
Never let anyone stand in line with spinning wheels, because they can throw gravel or ice and hurt someone. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-F13 | anchor: A02
Once moving on snow or ice, brake gently to test how slippery the road is and set your speed to match. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-F14 | anchor: A02
On snow or ice, stopping takes longer, so leave about eight to ten seconds between you and the vehicle ahead. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-F15 | anchor: A02
Brake gently and smoothly on slippery roads; slamming the brakes can cause a skid, and on very slick surfaces you pump the brakes unless your manual gives anti-lock instructions. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-F16 | anchor: A02
Bridges and overpasses freeze before the rest of the road, and patches of ice may remain even on cleared roads. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-F17 | anchor: A02
Do not use four-wheel drive on ice, where such vehicles can easily roll over; if you hit ice in four-wheel drive, lift your foot off the accelerator. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-F18 | anchor: A02
When rain starts, water mixes with road dust and oil into a slick film, wet leaves turn slippery, and stopping takes longer, so slow down and add following distance. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-F19 | anchor: A02
Do not use cruise control on wet pavement, because it keeps powering the wheels after traction is lost and can make you lose control. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-F20 | anchor: A02
Hydroplaning is when tires ride on water instead of the road; it can happen at any speed over 35 mph, and in a heavy storm tires can lose all contact at 55 mph. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-F21 | anchor: A02
If you think you are hydroplaning, ease off the accelerator and slow down without braking, which could cause a skid. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-F22 | anchor: A02
Prevent hydroplaning with good, deep-tread tires at proper pressure, slower speeds in rain, and no cruise control. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-F23 | anchor: A02
Four-wheel anti-lock brakes keep the wheels from locking in emergency braking, and you may feel the pedal pulse under hard braking. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-F24 | anchor: A03
With anti-lock brakes, keep firm, steady pressure on the pedal while you steer; do not pump the brakes, and do not be alarmed by mechanical noise or slight pulsing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec11-F25 | anchor: A03
A skid is handled the same way in front-wheel and rear-wheel drive vehicles: lift off the accelerator and do not hit the brakes. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec11-F26 | anchor: A03
In a skid, gently steer in the direction the rear wheels are sliding, without braking hard or jerking the wheel, which only makes it worse. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec11-F27 | anchor: A03
In fog, slow down, be ready to stop, and use low beams, because high beams make it harder to see. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec11-F28 | anchor: A03
If fog gets so thick that you cannot see, pull off the road, stop, and leave your lights and emergency flashers on. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec11-F29 | anchor: A03
The most important rule in any emergency is not to panic, and with power steering or a locking steering wheel, never turn off the ignition until fully stopped. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec11-F30 | anchor: A03
If the brake pedal sinks to the floor, pump it fast and hard several times, then apply the parking brake gradually and shift to a low gear while looking for a place to stop. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec11-F31 | anchor: A03
After a brake failure, get the vehicle off the road and call for help instead of driving to a garage. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec11-F32 | anchor: A04
In a tire blowout, grip the wheel firmly, lift off the accelerator without braking, and let the car slow until it is nearly stopped and off the road before braking. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-F33 | anchor: A04
After a blowout, turn on the emergency flashers and change the tire only if you can do it without putting yourself in danger. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-F34 | anchor: A04
If your wheels drop off the paved edge, hold the wheel tightly, ease off the gas without braking hard, and steer back once you have slowed, have control and the lane is clear. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-F35 | anchor: A04
If the steering fails, lift off the accelerator, let the vehicle slow on its own without braking until nearly stopped unless you must, and turn on the flashers. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-F36 | anchor: A04
If the headlights fail, try the dimmer or headlight switch, then switch on parking lights, flashers or turn signals and pull off the road with the flashers left on. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-F37 | anchor: A04
For a stuck accelerator, shift to neutral, brake, keep watching the road, warn others with the horn and flashers, and steer safely off the road. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-F38 | anchor: A04
With a stuck accelerator, turn off the ignition only after stopping and no longer needing to steer, since turning off the key locks the steering in many vehicles. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-F39 | anchor: A04
If the hood flies up or the wipers fail, roll down the window to see around the blockage, turn on the flashers and pull off the road. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-F40 | anchor: A04
If a vehicle comes at you head-on in your lane, slow down, pull to the right and sound your horn, but do not swerve into the left lane. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-F41 | anchor: A05
If your vehicle stalls on railroad tracks with a train coming, unbuckle, get out and away from the tracks, running toward the direction the train is coming from to avoid flying debris. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec11-F42 | anchor: A05
If you stall on the tracks with no train in sight, roll down the windows to listen, try to restart, and if that fails, shift to neutral and push the vehicle off. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec11-F43 | anchor: A05
The NTSB has found that 12- and 15-passenger vans are inherently unstable when loaded as designed with more than ten passengers, and it recommends special training for their drivers. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]

Misconceptions: snow tires or chains do not make normal speeds safe on snow or ice; cruise control is not safe on wet or icy roads; you do not pump anti-lock brakes; four-wheel drive does not make ice safe; high beams make fog worse, not better; in a stall with a train coming you run toward the train's direction, not away along its path.
Mnemonics: ice and snow, take it slow; in a skid, steer the way the back end is sliding; off the gas, not on the brakes, for blowouts, hydroplaning and skids.
Glossary: overdriving your headlights means driving too fast to stop within the lit distance; hydroplaning means tires riding on a film of water and losing traction; anti-lock braking system means brakes that keep the wheels from locking in hard stops; edgeline means the painted line at the right edge of the road; blowout means a sudden tire failure.
Dynamic facts: headlight hours and the wiper headlight rule are statutory and can change, and vehicle-specific braking advice depends on the owner's manual.
